question: The author's attitude towards policy debates is best described as:

group.title: Reading comprehension
group.setup: Economists often warn against judging a policy by its intentions rather than its results. A city that caps rents to help poor tenants may, over time, see landlords stop repairing buildings or convert flats into offices, shrinking the very supply the cap was meant to protect. Yet the opposite mistake is just as common: dismissing a policy because it has side effects, without asking whether the alternative is worse. A careful analyst therefore asks three questions: what happens if we act, what happens if we do not, and who bears the cost in each case. group.title: Reading comprehension
group.setup: Automation is usually discussed as a threat to jobs, but history suggests a more complicated picture. When automatic teller machines spread, many expected bank tellers to vanish. The lesson is not that technology never destroys work, for it plainly does, but that it changes which tasks are valuable. Workers who can move towards those tasks do well; those who cannot, or who are given no chance to learn, bear the cost of a progress that others enjoy.

question: Why might a district with more testing centres record more cases?

group.setup: A common error in reading statistics is to confuse a rise in reported cases with a rise in actual cases. question: What point does the last sentence make?

group.title: Reading comprehension
group.setup: Compound interest is often called the most powerful force in personal finance, yet its power is easy to underestimate because it works slowly at first. In the early years, a savings account seems to grow only by the money put into it; the interest feels trivial. Only after a decade or more does the interest earned each year begin to rival the deposits themselves. This is why those who start saving early, even in small amounts, often end up ahead of those who save larger sums later. The same arithmetic works against borrowers: an unpaid credit card balance grows in exactly the way a patient saver's account does.

explanation: 'The same arithmetic works against borrowers'.

group.title: Reading comprehension
group.setup: Economists often warn against judging a policy by its intentions rather than its results. A city that caps rents to help poor tenants may, over time, see landlords stop repairing buildings or convert flats into offices, shrinking the very supply the cap was meant to protect. Yet the opposite mistake is just as common: dismissing a policy because it has side effects, without asking whether the alternative is worse. A careful analyst therefore asks three questions: what happens if we act, what happens if we do not, and who bears the cost in each case.
